title: I Have a Confession to Make
subtitle: I've been spending time with Claude
body_html:
Dear readers,

I have slacked off. Now, in fairness, I warned you a while back that I was planning to slack off. It was to work on longer-form writing.

I have been working on longer-form writing. I have two books going on in the background. A little bit of a third too. I also edited the books I already have in print to ensure the formatting is even better.

I compressed the file sizes of the images in my e-book, so it takes up less space on your Kindle. (Amazon affiliate link). There is a print copy too.

I also connected my Google Mail account to some software to figure out who I knew and when I last talked to them.

If you're getting the idea that I'm spending time with somebody else, you're partially right. Friends, I've been having an affair with Claude Code.

I can imagine how you might feel—but Owen, we've developed such a parasocial relationship with you! Your nearly constant writing has kept us warm in the darkest of nights! This is true, I acknowledge it. I care so much about my readers, and I'm about to have a live in-person event where I won't be distracted by the magic of Claude Code, and we'll get to attend to you personally. I've even heard rumors that there will be merch. There will definitely be books. You can buy those books and read them, even if your computer doesn't have battery power. That's how much I care about you.

The Live-Action Version of this Newsletter, RAMHT 2026 SF, is coming up on May 16th, 2026!

Get a ticket now—it’s free if you ask. Just email us at ramhtevents@gmail.com for your free code.

Get Tickets to RAMHT 2026 SF

I also don't write this newsletter’s text using artificial intelligence, beyond the ancient tech currently behind Siri. You see, it was artificial intelligence that unlocked my ability to write this column so rapidly in the first place. Before the voice transcribing abilities of Siri, I really didn't bother with writing much. I hate typing; I'm not very good at it. I have arthritis, no thank you. I just found it off-putting. Dreadful, draining.

And now, here I am, writing things all the time. It's because of AI. It's not because of generative AI—those chatbots that crank out endless text that all feel soulless— because it is. By the way, you'll notice it is not exactly an em-dash. I added that myself.

Or rather, as I dictated, Siri did it.

But now I've been spending time with somebody else. That somebody else is not somebody. It's a robot. It's called Claude Code. And it lets us make things that are pointless. Some of them will have a point. Today, I'm gonna recommend how you should start using Claude code, if it's not yet part of your life, to get the point.

I'm not saying you have to use AI in your day-to-day life. I'm saying it's a good idea to have a sense of how AI tools like Claude are gonna change how other people are doing things. So you can be prepared in your own mind!

You might've heard Claude Cowork before. I'm here to tell you. It's kind of pointless. It's not that it doesn't have a point; it's got a pretty user interface. But Claude Code can do everything that Claude cowork can do, with just a less nice user interface.

For your Author, as a healthcare professional, there was no choice, because until we got an enterprise-level subscription, which is wildly expensive, at Radial, I could not use Claude for things that I really wanted to use Claude for. Nothing for me, anyway, because most of what I do in my day, my workday, touches on protected health information. This requires a specific contract with a software vendor for zero data retention. I also need a business associate agreement. I need HIPAA compliance.

I need to protect my patients' privacy. Until that was addressed, none of this fancy AI mumbo jumbo could do much for me. But now that day has come.

So here's how I think everyone could get started with automated agents, so they can understand how other people are gonna be using automated agents.

An agent is basically a Chatbot that can access other stuff on a computer. The chat bots of a year ago couldn't click a button, interface with your web browser, or move files around on your computer, that kind of stuff. It's easy to forget, but all that clicking buttons is really just a lot of software that creates a bridge between a human brain and a robot brain. These robot brains live in the terminal. It has a command line; you type a command, and it does something. When you want to move a file, we've all taken it for granted that you basically click on the file and drag it to where you want it to go. But there's a translation layer behind that physical movement depicted on the screen and what actually happens, which is there's an underlying terminal command “mv” which then tells the software, which doesn't have a mouse, to move a file from one place where it currently is to another place where it will be, and we're basically writing code by moving our hand on that mouse.

A lot of our brains think about user interface, because human users think about user interface, but robots don't. They think about code. They don't really think. But if they did, they'd think about code.

I'm gonna encourage you to get started in this future of automated things by doing something pretty pointless. Pick a task in your life, maybe it's figuring out when it's time to water the plants. This is the sort of task that humans are pretty bad at, on average. Other things get in the way, our attention is re-allocated to crucial issues of the day, and we forget to water a plant. Robots don't have attention. Robots don't get distracted. The robots will just tell you it's time to water the plant, or not water the plant. So you could tell it what plants you have, or you could even take pictures of the plants, and feed those into the computer, and then correct it if it gets it wrong, which by the way it does all the time right now.

Expect mistakes, that's one lesson.

But you could give it the two, or three, or 10, or 20 plants in your house—did I mention we have a lot of plants in my house?

And you could ask it to create a schedule for ideal watering for those plants, and then have that schedule run every day. If you are connected to your email, I can even send you an email in the morning about which plant should be watered and any Special plant watering and concerns you haven't thought about.

All of this could've been done with a piece of paper, a clock, a calendar, and good sense. It might've taken you a little bit of time to look something up in a book. The point is not that you can't do this in some other way; the point is to understand how and, by doing this simple task, you're creating a model of how other people— people with power, influence, and enterprise subscriptions to these things— are gonna be using these tools to interact with the world, and, sometimes, you.

Scammers are gonna be using these tools to learn all about us. They're doing it right now, and they're getting data from the dark web, and they're using it to craft endlessly more appealing scams to seperate you and your money.

The only good news about the automated future is that it's at least possible that all that money they're robbing you of won't matter that much. My friend Michelle Bernabe calls this future “luxury automated communism.” This originally was somebody's investment thesis, but I can't remember who.

I'm not gonna bother to look it up. If it's important to you, you can take this entire article, put it into a chatbot, and ask it to answer that question for you. A nice thing, at least right now, is that you can't be sure it would be right. Some tasks benefit from having “on average” correctish execution. Others can't be wrong, ever. Or it will be life or death. I live in that world, the world of medical devices, the world of “error not allowed.” Medicine needs to follow some pretty deterministic rules for its devices, which is ironic because it's human practitioners who are given tremendous latitude.

Today, I'm gonna encourage you to take the plunge. Consider building a little Claude Code agent for yourself. Or I guess you could use OpenClaw. Or any number of other tools. I just think Claude is the best tool I've used yet, and I'm sure whoever's leading the pack for any given task is gonna bounce back-and-forth in the very near future.

It's either gonna end up like the Top college list—they rotate the top three to keep us buying next year's report on who the top college is… or it's not. Maybe there won't be top colleges in the future, because no one will think it makes sense to go to college.

Try to do something. Try to do something that does something for you. Try to do something that's within your risk tolerance. Don't do things that you wouldn't be comfortable letting an error-prone robot do. It will make misunderstandings, which are important to understand. Those are important to feel in your soul. You need a sense of how AI will be wrong to navigate the future in a way that's less brain-dead than we do now. But you should try to do something.

Now, I'm gonna take time away from writing this column, so I can go back to using Claude code, because I gotta check who works for me, and when their licenses are expiring, so I can automate the process of reminding them to resubmit those licenses, before I can automate the process of actually just resubmitting the license applications with their sign off. Etc., etc.

Veni, vidi, automavi.
